claims.text: In low-dimensional non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloys, magnetocaloric response and hysteresis are governed partly by nanoscale structural disorder and interfacial magnetic anisotropy.
Nanoscale structural disorder and interfacial magnetic anisotropy alter magnetic-domain switching dynamics.
Local heat-transfer limitations govern the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-field cooling cycles.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of the low-dimensional samples accentuates temperature gradients and slows thermal equilibration.
As-deposited nanoscale FeMnNiGeSi-type films or nanoribbons exhibit bulk-type magnetocaloric behavior, potentially with degraded performance in reduced dimensions.
Au or Cu can serve as a high-thermal-conductivity capping layer.
A high-thermal-conductivity cap improves interfacial heat transfer during magnetic cycling.
The cap may mitigate surface-induced strain effects.
Nanoscale grain-boundary disorder influences local magnetic-domain alignment.
Surface or interface thermal resistance influences heat-dissipation rates.
Improved heat transfer from the cap reduces local temperature gradients.
Reduced temperature gradients permit more homogeneous magnetic-domain switching.
More homogeneous magnetic-domain switching reduces hysteresis.
The cap may alleviate strain-induced variations in magnetic anisotropy.
Reducing strain-induced anisotropy variations stabilizes the magnetocaloric response.
Capped samples will have a smaller magnetic hysteresis-loop area than uncapped as-deposited samples.
Capped samples will show a larger or more consistent magnetocaloric temperature change than uncapped as-deposited samples.
The uncapped baseline displays pronounced hysteresis under low-applied-field conditions.
The uncapped baseline has a less reliable magnetocaloric response under low-applied-field conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies to approximately 100 nm samples cycled near room temperature at applied fields below 100 mT.
